title: The Calamity of Damascus
intro: Ahmad Shawqi wrote this poem after the French shelled and bombed the quarters of Damascus in October 1925, during the Syrian revolt that Druze leaders in the Hawran had started that summer; al-Shawqiyyat says it was recited in January 1926 at a benefit for the Syrian victims held at the Azbakiyya Garden theatre in Cairo, and Rashid Rida printed it in his journal al-Manar. It opens with a greeting to Damascus and the memory of a visit among young men of the city who knew his poems by heart, then turns to the news of the disaster, the city's glories from the Umayyads to Saladin, and the night of the shelling, when the women fled through the burning gardens. He then reproaches France with its own revolution, urges the Syrians to give up dreams and empty titles and to stand together, and ends with the price of freedom and a blessing on the people of Damascus; five closing lines in praise of the Druze are not recited here. Ali al-Tantawi recalls reciting it to his school in Damascus while the revolt was still being fought, to applause at every line; he wrote that some of its lines “went about among people as proverbs do”, and called the line on the red door of freedom the heart of the poem.

translation: A greeting gentler than the east wind over the Barada,
and tears that will not be dried, Damascus.
1.sharh: He opens with a greeting softer than the breeze that blows along the city's river, and with tears that will not stop: tenderness and grief together, before he says what has happened.

translation: My pen and my rhymes plead their excuse:
the calamity is too great for any words to reach.
2.sharh: Before he begins he asks pardon for falling short: what has happened to Damascus is so vast that any description must fail it. Ali al-Tantawi remarks that he described it well all the same.

translation: And a memory whose thoughts keep my heart
forever turning towards you, and beating.
3.sharh: He carries a memory of Damascus that never leaves him; whenever it comes to mind, his heart turns to the city like someone looking back, and beats faster.

translation: From all that the nights have hurled at you
I carry wounds that run deep in the heart.
4.sharh: The blows that fate has dealt the city have struck him too. “The nights” is the usual Arabic way of naming fate and its turns.

translation: I came to you when the late afternoon was aglow
and your face was open, its features laughing.
5.sharh: He remembers a visit to Damascus in the golden light before sunset, and pictures the city as a woman with a bright, laughing face, as it was before the disaster.

translation: Beneath your gardens the rivers flowed,
and your hills were full of leaves and doves.
6.sharh: The rivers running beneath the gardens echo the Quran's picture of paradise. In Arabic “leaves” and “doves” (awraq, wurq) share their letters, a play the translation cannot keep.

translation: Around me were young men, noble and fair of face,
who had run to the farthest goals of merit and come first.
7.sharh: He recalls the young men of Damascus who gathered round him, outstanding in every virtue. “Goals” and “first” come from horse racing: they ran the whole course and won.

translation: On their palates sat eloquent poets,
and in their sides broad-mouthed orators.
8.sharh: Each of these young men had a poet and an orator living inside him, always ready on the tongue: eloquence was in their nature, not something they had to learn.

translation: They recited my poems: marvel at verse
that crowds recite in every quarter.
9.sharh: The young men knew his poems by heart, and he marvels that the verse of a poet from Egypt is recited in every quarter of Damascus.

translation: I pressed on their pride until the lions' noses
blazed and the ridges of their noses flared.
10.sharh: His poems stirred their pride until it flared up like a lion's anger. In Arabic the nose stands for pride and the refusal to be humbled, so blazing noses are pride roused.

translation: And every free and proud man, with the noble blood
of the Umayyads in him, cried out against the bit.
11.sharh: Each proud young man protested against the restraint put on him, as a thoroughbred chafes at the bit. The Umayyads ruled their empire from Damascus, and their nobility runs in the city's blood.

translation: God curse the news that followed, report after report,
bringing a friend's ear what is hard to bear.
12.sharh: The poem turns from memory to the present: report after report of the disaster reaches him, and he curses the news for what it brings to one who loves the city.

translation: The post spells it out to the world in detail,
and the telegraph sums it up for the far horizons.
13.sharh: Letters and newspapers give the full story, and the telegraph sends it in a few words across the world. The line sets detail against summary, and pairs barid, “post”, with barq, two words built on the same letters.

translation: So dreadful were the events in it
it might almost be taken for a fable, though it is true.
14.sharh: The news is so terrible that a listener could take it for a tale someone made up, yet every word of it is true.

translation: It was said the monuments of history were levelled,
it was said that ruin and fire had struck them.
15.sharh: Reports said the city's historic buildings were destroyed and burned. Ali al-Tantawi recalls that the French burned the finest quarter, between two great markets, which has been called al-Hariqa, “the Fire”, ever since.

translation: Damascus, were you not a wet-nurse to Islam?
A nurse who stands as a parent is not to be wronged.
16.sharh: Damascus nursed Islam as its first imperial capital. In Arabic custom a wet-nurse has a mother's rights, so failing her would be like a child's betrayal of a parent.

translation: Saladin is your crown: no head has been adorned,
no parting of the hair marked, with anything finer.
17.sharh: Saladin, who died in Damascus, is the crown on the city's head; no head ever wore a finer one. The parting of the hair stands for the head where a crown sits.

translation: Every civilisation that grew tall on the earth
has a root that runs to your lofty trees.
18.sharh: Damascus is pictured as an ancient, towering tree: every civilisation that has grown tall anywhere on earth has a root that reaches back to it and draws on what the city gave.

translation: Your sky is a book of the ornaments of the past,
and your earth a parchment of history's ornaments.
19.sharh: Everything in Damascus, above and below, bears witness to its history, as if sky and ground were pages written over with the glories of the past.

translation: You built the great state, and a kingdom
whose two civilisations left a dust no one could break through.
20.sharh: Damascus founded the Umayyad caliphate, whose civilisation flourished first in Syria and then in Spain, and no rival ever caught up with either.

translation: It had banners and a wedding feast in Syria,
and the drums of its good news were beaten in al-Andalus.
21.sharh: The Umayyad realm stretched from Damascus to Spain: the celebration began in Syria and its drums were heard at the far end of the Mediterranean, in al-Andalus.

translation: The abodes of paradise, alas, what has struck them?
Is it true that they are wiped away? Is it true?
22.sharh: He asks in disbelief what has happened to the homes of Damascus, a city he calls paradise, and repeats the question like a man who cannot accept the news.

translation: Are the chambers of the gardens still set in rows?
Does their bliss keep its order as it did yesterday?
23.sharh: He wonders whether the garden houses of Damascus still stand in their ordered rows and whether life in them still runs as it did, borrowing the Quran's picture of the lofty chambers of paradise.

translation: And where are the ivory beauties of the inner rooms,
now their curtained alcoves are rent and their hangings torn?
24.sharh: He asks after the sheltered women of Damascus, beautiful as carved figures in their private rooms, now that the curtains that hid them are torn away.

translation: They came out, with fire on every side of the grove,
and behind the grove fledglings still being fed.
25.sharh: The women fled their homes through the burning gardens with their small children behind them, still young enough to be fed like nestlings. Al-Tantawi reads it so: the houses fell on them, and they came out with fire all round and their children in danger.

translation: Whenever they sought safety down one road,
roads of death reached it before them.
26.sharh: There was no escape: every road the women tried to flee by, death had already reached first. The one road to safety is set against the many roads of death.

translation: On a night where, behind its sky, shells and deaths
flashed and thundered.
27.sharh: The bombardment came from above in the dark, the shells flashing like lightning that blinds and crashing like thunder. The French used both artillery and aircraft against the city.

translation: When the iron stormed, one horizon flamed red
on its sides, and another turned black.
28.sharh: As the shelling grew heavier, part of the sky glowed red with fire and part went black with smoke, so the night over Damascus is painted in those two colours.

translation: Ask the one who terrified your fair women after midnight:
is there any difference between his heart and rock?
29.sharh: Addressing Damascus, he calls on the city to question the man who frightened its women in the night; his heart, the line implies, is stone.

translation: Colonisers, however soft their words,
have hearts like stones that never soften.
30.sharh: However gently colonial powers speak, their hearts are hard. Ali al-Tantawi, who recited this poem as a schoolboy, comments that they dress the stones in silk.

translation: A warmonger, all arrogance and folly,
struck you with his rashness, and struck France too.
31.sharh: The commander who ordered the bombardment harmed France as much as Damascus, since his rash cruelty disgraced his own country in the eyes of the world.

translation: When people come to him demanding their rights,
he says, “A gang of rebels who have broken ranks.”
32.sharh: He calls anyone who asks for their rights a gang of outlaws, turning a just demand into a rebellion, as occupiers have always done.

translation: France knows the blood of revolutionaries,
and knows that it is light, and right.
33.sharh: France was itself remade by revolution, so it knows what the blood of rebels is worth. The poet turns France's own history against it.

translation: It ran through her own land, bearing life
like the rain pouring from the sky, and bearing bounty.
34.sharh: The blood of France's own revolutionaries gave the country new life, as rain revives dead earth and makes it bear. Blood shed for freedom, he implies, is never wasted.

translation: A country whose young men died so that it might live,
and perished for their people so that they might endure.
35.sharh: France, of all nations, knows that freedom is bought with the lives of the young, because its own young men paid that price. Its own history should have taught it to understand the Syrians.

translation: Peoples were set free on her spears:
how then can they be enslaved on her spears?
36.sharh: France's revolutionary armies once carried liberty to other peoples; he asks how the same spears can now be used to enslave them. Repeating “on her spears” sets France's past against its present.

translation: Sons of Syria, cast away vain hopes,
throw off your dreams, throw them off.
37.sharh: He turns from France to the Syrians themselves: freedom will not come from wishing, or from waiting for the occupier to be just, and he repeats the command, “throw them off”, for force.

translation: For it is one of the tricks of politics that you be lured
by titles of rule, when they are slavery.
38.sharh: He warns them not to be won over by princely titles handed out by the occupier, which are servitude in disguise. The word for slavery, riqq, echoes raqq, “parchment”, in line 19.

translation: How often you see a humbled man hold his head high,
the way a crucified man's neck leans to one side.
39.sharh: A man who accepts office under the occupier may carry himself proudly, but the tilt of his head is like that of a crucified man: the posture of defeat, not pride.

translation: Rifts in a kingdom open and then close,
but no rift closes for those who are divided.
40.sharh: A state can recover from the troubles that tear it, but not from division among its people. The Arabic word, fatq, is a rent in cloth. Al-Tantawi counts this among the lines that became proverbs.

translation: I give this counsel though we live in different lands,
for in our cares we are all the East.
41.sharh: He speaks as an Egyptian to Syrians: their countries differ, but the peoples of the East share the same troubles. Al-Tantawi reads it as an answer to anyone who asks what right an outsider has to advise them.

translation: And if our countries differ, we are united
by one eloquence and one speech.
42.sharh: What binds Egypt and Syria across their borders is the Arabic language they share, its eloquence and its speech. Al-Tantawi adds that language alone unites no one unless faith goes with it.

translation: You stand between death and life:
if you seek lasting bliss, then suffer.
43.sharh: The Syrians stand between death and life, and lasting happiness will only come through hardship accepted now. Al-Tantawi quotes it first among the poem's lines that passed into common use.

translation: Homelands have, in the blood of every free man,
a favour granted long ago and a debt now due.
44.sharh: A free man owes his homeland his blood. The homeland raised him, a favour done long ago; now the debt has fallen due, and he must repay it even with his life.

translation: Who will pour death for others and drink it,
if the free will not drink it and pour it?
45.sharh: War is pictured as pouring and drinking the cup of death. If free men will not fight, kill and be killed, no one will.

translation: Nothing builds kingdoms like those who give their lives;
nothing else brings rights near or makes them stand.
46.sharh: States are built, and rights won and secured, only by the sacrifice of those who die for them. Rights, he means, are not granted on request; they have to be paid for.

translation: In the slain there is life for generations to come,
in the captives a ransom for them, and their freedom.
47.sharh: Those killed in the struggle give life to the generations after them, and the suffering of those taken captive buys those generations' freedom. What looks like loss now is the price of others' liberty.

translation: Red freedom has a door
that is knocked on by every blood-stained hand.
48.sharh: Freedom is won only through sacrifice: its door opens to hands stained with blood, which is why it is called red. Al-Tantawi called it the poem's centrepiece, though he thought it weakly put together.

translation: May the Lord of majesty reward you, sons of Damascus;
the glory of the East begins with Damascus.
49.sharh: He blesses the people of Damascus for their struggle and puts their city at the head of the East's glory. The city's name is the rhyme word here, as it was in the opening line.

translation: You stood by your brother on the day of his ordeal,
and every brother owes his brother help.
50.sharh: The people of Damascus rose to support their brothers in their trial, as brothers should: their help was a duty, not a favour. The next line in the diwan, not recited here, names those brothers.

1.1.3.head: الصَّبا
1.1.3.meaning: Saba: the east wind, gentle and longed-for in Arabic love poetry.

1.1.4.meaning: Barada: the river of Damascus, whose branches water the Ghouta, the gardens around the city.

2.1.2.head: اليَراعَة
2.1.2.meaning: Yara'a: a reed pen, and so the pen.

5.1.2.head: الأَصيل
5.1.2.meaning: Asil: the late afternoon, between the afternoon prayer and sunset.

6.2.4.head: وُرق
6.2.4.meaning: Wurq: grey doves, plural of warqa'.

8.1.2.head: لَهَوات
8.1.2.meaning: Lahawat: the soft palate at the back of the mouth.

10.1.1.head: غَمَزَ
10.1.1.meaning: Pressed, as one presses a spear shaft to test its strength.

10.2.4.head: المَدَقّ
10.2.4.meaning: Madaqq: the ridge of the nose, as the edition's note explains.

11.1.3.head: الشَّكيمَة
11.1.3.meaning: Shakima: the bar of a bridle's bit that lies across a horse's mouth.

11.2.3.head: أُمَيَّة
11.2.3.meaning: Umayya: the Umayyads, the caliphs who ruled from Damascus.

12.1.1.head: لَحا
12.1.1.meaning: Lahaha Allah: “God strip it”, a curse.

13.2.4.meaning: Barq: lightning; here the electric telegraph.

16.2.4.head: عَقَّ
16.2.4.meaning: Wronged as an undutiful child wrongs a parent, the sin Arabic calls uquq.

17.1.1-2.meaning: Salah al-Din (Saladin, d. 589 AH, 1193 CE): the sultan who grew up in Damascus, retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 583 AH (1187 CE) and died in Damascus.

20.1.2-3.meaning: “The great state”: the Umayyad caliphate, ruled from Damascus.

20.2.3-4.meaning: “Its dust is not split”: said of a horse no one can overtake.

21.1.2.head: الشّام
21.1.2.meaning: Al-Sham: Greater Syria, with Damascus its chief city.

21.2.2.head: أَندَلُس
21.2.2.meaning: Al-Andalus: Muslim Spain, where Abd al-Rahman al-Dakhil founded an Umayyad state after the dynasty fell in the east.

24.1.2.meaning: Duma: carved figures of ivory or marble, to which beautiful women are compared.

24.1.5.head: حِجال
24.1.5.meaning: Hijal: curtained canopies, like the one prepared for a bride.

25.1.4.head: الأَيك
25.1.4.meaning: Ayk: dense, tangled trees, a grove.

25.2.4.head: زَقَّ
25.2.4.meaning: Fed beak to beak, as a bird feeds its chicks.

29.1.4.head: غيد
29.1.4.meaning: Ghid: graceful women, soft and supple.

29.1.6.head: وَهن
29.1.6.meaning: Wahn: around midnight, or an hour after.

31.1.4.meaning: France, which had occupied Syria in 1920.

31.2.1-2.meaning: “Brother of war”: a warmonger. He means General Sarrail, the French high commissioner who ordered the bombardment.

32.2.4.head: شَقَّ
32.2.4.meaning: “Split”: short for splitting the staff of obedience, that is, rebelling.

34.2.1-2.meaning: “Like the pouring of the sky”: like heavy rain.

39.1.2.head: صَيَد
39.1.2.meaning: Sayad: a neck held stiff and the head raised in pride.

44.2.1.meaning: “A hand”: a favour or kindness done.

47.2.5.head: عِتق
47.2.5.meaning: Itq: freedom; properly, the freeing of a slave.

50.1.4.head: أَخ
50.1.4.meaning: He means the Druze, among whom the Syrian revolt began in 1925 under Sultan al-Atrash.
